question_text: Define symmetric and skew symmetric matrices.

recall_prompt: Say both definitions, and say what skew symmetry forces the diagonal entries to be.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Define a symmetric matrix
steps.margin_note: First mark. Write the condition in symbols, Aᵀ = A, and in entries, aⱼᵢ = aᵢⱼ. Either form earns it; both together are safest.
lines: A square matrix A = [aᵢⱼ] is called symmetric
if Aᵀ = A, that is aⱼᵢ = aᵢⱼ for all i and j.
Example: the matrix with rows (1, 2) and (2, 5).

recall.must_convey: That a square matrix is symmetric when it equals its own transpose, Aᵀ = A.
accept: a square matrix is symmetric if it equals its transpose
symmetric means A equals A transpose
the entry in row j column i equals the entry in row i column j
symmetric ante A equals A transpose

steps.why: Symmetry is a reflection across the principal diagonal, so the condition ties each entry to the one in the mirrored position. The word square belongs in the definition, because only a square matrix can equal its own transpose.
common_mistakes: Writing Aᵀ = −A, which is the skew symmetric condition.
Saying only that the matrix looks the same, with no condition.
steps.memory_tip: Symmetric: fold along the principal diagonal and the two halves match, Aᵀ = A.

steps.label: Define a skew symmetric matrix
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Aᵀ = −A. The line aᵢᵢ = −aᵢᵢ is worth writing: it shows why every principal diagonal entry has to be 0.
lines: A square matrix A = [aᵢⱼ] is called skew
symmetric if Aᵀ = −A, that is aⱼᵢ = −aᵢⱼ.
Putting j = i gives aᵢᵢ = −aᵢᵢ, so 2aᵢᵢ = 0.
So every principal diagonal entry is 0.
Example: the matrix with rows (0, 3) and (−3, 0).

recall.must_convey: That a square matrix is skew symmetric when Aᵀ = −A, and that this forces every diagonal entry to be zero.
accept: skew symmetric means A transpose equals minus A
the entry in row j column i is minus the entry in row i column j
putting j equal to i gives a i i equals minus a i i so the diagonal is zero
skew symmetric ante A transpose equals minus A, diagonal anni zero
every principal diagonal entry must be zero

steps.why: The sign flip is the whole difference between the two definitions, and it has one consequence a marker looks for: a diagonal entry is its own mirror image, so it must equal its own negative and therefore be zero.
common_mistakes: Writing Aᵀ = A for the skew symmetric case.
Giving an example with a non-zero diagonal entry.
Saying the diagonal is zero without showing why.
steps.memory_tip: Skew symmetric: same mirror, opposite sign, so the diagonal has to be 0.
